pr.title: match lowering: sort `Eq` candidates in the failure case too
pr.description:
This is a slight tweak to MIR gen of matches. Take a match like:
```rust
match (s, flag) {
    ("a", _) if foo() => 1,
    ("b", true) => 2,
    ("a", false) => 3,
    (_, true) => 4,
    _ => 5,
}
```
If we switch on `s == "a"`, the first candidate matches, and we learn almost nothing about the second candidate. So there's a choice:
1. (what we do today) stop sorting candidates, keep the "b" case grouped with everything below. This could allow us to be clever here and test on `flag == true` next.
2. (what this PR does) sort "b" into the failure case. The "b" will be alone (fewer opportunities for picking a good test), but that means the two "a" cases require a single test.

Today, we aren't clever in which tests we pick, so this is an unambiguous win. In a future where we pick tests better, idk. Grouping tests as much as possible feels like a generally good strategy.

This was proposed in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/29623 (9 years ago :D)
pr.author: Nadrieril

processing.reason: PR #122459 is explicitly an optimization of match-lowering candidate sorting, not a semantic bug fix. The historical original leaves an unequal `TestCase::Constant` candidate unclassified (so it remains in the failure case and the same equality test may be emitted twice), while the transformed version classifies it as `TestBranch::Failure` and sorts it directly into the failure case. Both revisions make the same match decisions and return identical values for every concrete scrutinee/guard input; the only observable difference in the supplied regression is redundant MIR equality testing (`constant_eq` testing `"a"` twice versus once). Reconstructing these as ordinary Rust functions cannot produce different defined return values without inventing unrelated behavior, so there is no valid source-grounded counterexample pair.

analysis.originalLogic: In match lowering's candidate sorting, the `(TestKind::Eq { value: test_val, .. }, TestCase::Constant { value: case_val })` case only handled equal constants: the source had `// FIXME(#29623): return `Some(1)` when the values are different.` followed by a guard `if test_val == case_val => { fully_matched = true; Some(TestBranch::Success) }`. When the constants differed, that arm did not apply, so the constant candidate was not classified as failing the equality test and remained unsorted for the failure edge.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: Historical behavior: for an `Eq` test against a `Constant` candidate whose value is different, do not return `Some(TestBranch::Failure)` and do not set `fully_matched = false`; leave the candidate unclassified so it stays in the failure case along with later candidates. In the supplied `constant_eq` example this led to testing the string `"a"` twice in the generated MIR.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR match lowering where a candidate is tested with `TestKind::Eq` and another candidate is `TestCase::Constant`, especially matches over tuples/strings where the same scrutinee constant appears in multiple arms mixed with guards, booleans, and catch-all arms. The motivating example is `match (s, flag) { ("a", _) if foo() => 1, ("b", true) => 2, ("a", false) => 3, (_, true) => 4, _ => 5, }`. The regression input uses `match (s, b) { ("a", _) if true => 1, ("b", true) => 2, ("a", true) => 3, (_, true) => 4, _ => 5, }`.
analysis.summary: Historical match-lowering optimization: when an `Eq` test is compared with a `Constant` candidate, sort unequal constants directly into the failure case instead of leaving them unclassified. This avoids redundant equality tests, e.g. testing `"a"` twice in `sort_candidates.constant_eq`. The PR is an optimization, not a confirmed bug fix; MIR is observed at the `SimplifyCfg-initial` checkpoint.
analysis.trigger: A match-lowering test is `TestKind::Eq { value: test_val, .. }` and the candidate is `TestCase::Constant { value: case_val }` with `test_val != case_val`. The optimization applies by returning `TestBranch::Failure` for that candidate and setting `fully_matched = false`.
preconditions: The test kind is an equality test (`TestKind::Eq`), not a range or other test kind.
The equality-test value and the candidate constant differ; equal values remain `TestBranch::Success` with `fully_matched = true`.
Candidate sorting has not already decided the candidate's branch.
pitfalls: Do not generalize this failure classification to non-equality tests such as ranges; the changed arm is specifically `TestKind::Eq` against `TestCase::Constant`.

Distinguish the historical unclassified behavior from a semantic miscompile: the PR describes an optimization and says the old approach 'could allow us to be clever here', but today's test selection is not clever, so leaving the candidate unsorted causes redundant testing.
Do not infer correctness from renamed test files alone; compare the actual MIR value assignments and control-flow edges in the decoded revisions.

The changed compiler code is in match lowering (`rustc_mir_build/src/build/matches/test.rs`), while the supplied pass ID evidence is the `SimplifyCfg-initial` MIR checkpoint; do not misattribute the code change to the `SimplifyCfg` implementation itself.
analysis.testStrategy: Use MIR-opt tests at the `SimplifyCfg-initial` checkpoint. Add a `constant_eq` source match where the same constant appears in multiple arms and assert with FileCheck that it is tested only once: `// CHECK: [[a:_.*]] = const "a";` followed by `// CHECK-NOT: {{_.*}} = const "a";`. Compare old and new MIR: the old output had two `<str as PartialEq>::eq(..., const "a")` calls; the corrected output tests `"a"` once and sorts `"b"` into the failure path. Also retain the `disjoint_ranges` case and verify the CFG shortcut for a guard failure, using directives such as `// CHECK: switchInt(_2) -> [0: [[jump:bb.*]], otherwise: {{bb.*}}];`, `// CHECK: [[jump]]: {`, and `// CHECK-NEXT: _0 = const 3_u32;`. No compiler execution or reproduction is claimed here.
